fit_paragraphs.text: Prof. Fazeli's MMint Lab addresses the exact intersection I want to pursue. ViTaSCOPE [paper:W4414050430] estimates in-hand pose by fusing vision and tactile signals — a direct extension of the piezoresistive fabric skin I built as an undergraduate that detects slip in 60 ms across 64 taxels [lib:cv]. His diffusion-based behavior cloning work maps onto the diffusion-policy pipeline I developed at IISc, where 40 demonstrations per task reached 78% success on cup stacking on a $1,800 arm [lib:cv]. The lab's stated focus on assistive care [advisor:Nima Fazeli] aligns with my secondary goal of household robotics for elderly care [lib:interests]. I would like to extend vision–tactile fusion to deformable objects such as cloth and food within Prof. Fazeli's lab.

Prof. Goyal's work on learning precise manipulation from few demonstrations is central to what I do. RVT-2 [paper:W4402354093] achieves sample-efficient manipulation via 3D multi-view representations, and 3D-MVP [paper:W4413144893] shows how spatial pretraining improves generalisation across object instances — both directly relevant to my goal of diffusion policies that generalise across instances and lighting with as few as 40 demonstrations [lib:cv][lib:interests]. My real-to-sim reconstruction work at TCS Research, which reduced the sim-to-real drop from 41 to 17 percentage points [lib:cv], could complement his 3D pretraining framework. I would want to investigate whether photo-based scene reconstruction can serve as a low-cost alternative to manual 3D asset creation for RVT-style policies.

Prof. Berenson's ARM Lab focuses on generalizable trajectory learning and deformable object manipulation, which maps directly onto two of my core interests [advisor:Dmitry Berenson]. The work on learning a generalizable trajectory sampling distribution for MPC [paper:W4392207744] addresses policy generalisation under uncertainty — a challenge I encountered when transferring diffusion policies from a reconstructed kitchen simulation to a real counter [lib:cv]. Constrained Stein Variational Trajectory Optimization [paper:W4400644189] also speaks to my secondary interest in safety constraints for learned policies [lib:interests]. My experience with towel-folding policies and a 64-taxel fabric tactile skin [lib:cv] would contribute to the lab's ongoing deformable object manipulation agenda.

Prof. Bucher's work on zero-shot transfer to unstructured environments is relevant to making manipulation policies robust across real homes. VLFM [paper:W4401417061] demonstrates semantic navigation that transfers without re-training by grounding vision-language representations to frontier maps, and the zero-shot instruction-following paper [paper:W4404390404] extends this to object-centric tasks. My TCS Research internship showed that realistic scene reconstruction reduces sim-to-real gaps [lib:cv]; combining that with zero-shot transfer methods from Prof. Bucher's lab could yield policies that deploy in novel household environments without any real-world fine-tuning [lib:interests]. The lab's active recruiting [advisor:Bernadette Bucher] also suggests capacity for new PhD students.

sop.text:
I want to build manipulation systems that work in ordinary homes using hardware families can afford. Reaching that goal requires solving three interlocked problems: learning from few demonstrations, perceiving deformable objects through touch as well as vision, and closing the sim-to-real gap cheaply.

My M.Tech work at IISc directly targets the first two. Advised by Prof. Meera Natarajan, I built a diffusion-policy pipeline on a $1,800 six-DoF arm [lib:cv]. With 40 teleoperated demonstrations per task the policy reached 78% success on cup stacking and 61% on towel folding, outperforming a behavior-cloning baseline by 34 and 32 percentage points respectively [lib:cv]. The towel result matters most to me: deformable objects expose the limits of vision alone. As an undergraduate at BITS Pilani I built a piezoresistive fabric tactile skin — 64 taxels, slip detected in 60 ms at 91% reliability — that suggests a low-cost path forward [lib:cv]. A first-authored workshop paper combining these directions is currently under review [lib:cv].

At TCS Research I worked on the sim-to-real half of the problem. Reconstructing a kitchen counter from twelve phone photos reduced the sim-to-real success drop from 41 percentage points to 17, without any domain-randomisation tuning [lib:cv]. That 24-point recovery shows that cheap scene reconstruction can substitute for expensive real-world data collection.

At Michigan I want to combine these threads under Prof. Nima Fazeli in the MMint Lab. ViTaSCOPE [paper:W4414050430] fuses vision and tactile signals for in-hand pose estimation — the precise capability my fabric skin prototype approached — and the lab's diffusion-based behavior cloning work aligns directly with my IISc pipeline [advisor:Nima Fazeli]. Prof. Dmitry Berenson's ARM Lab is a second strong fit: his work on generalizable trajectory sampling [paper:W4392207744] addresses the policy-distribution question I keep running into with deformable tasks, and his safety-constrained trajectory optimization [paper:W4400644189] speaks to my secondary interest in safe learned policies [lib:interests].

Longer term, I aim to deploy these systems as assistive tools for elderly care in Indian households — low-cost, tactile-aware robots that handle laundry, prepare soft foods, and support daily living [lib:interests]. Michigan's Robotics program, with its depth in manipulation, perception, and learning, is the right environment to pursue this.

emails.subject: Prospective PhD student interested in visuo-tactile manipulation — Fall 2027
emails.body:
Dear Prof. Fazeli,

I am Arjun Mehta, an M.Tech student in Robotics at the Indian Institute of Science (CGPA 9.4/10), applying to Michigan's PhD program for Fall 2027 [lib:profile].

Your recent paper ViTaSCOPE [paper:W4414050430], which estimates in-hand pose by fusing vision and tactile signals, is closely related to work I have been building toward. As an undergraduate I constructed a 64-taxel piezoresistive fabric skin for slip detection, and at IISc I developed a diffusion-policy pipeline on a sub-$2k arm that reaches 78% success on cup stacking from 40 demonstrations [lib:cv]. A first-authored workshop paper on this work is currently under review [lib:cv]. I would like to extend vision–tactile fusion to deformable objects such as cloth and food, which I see as a natural next step given the MMint Lab's direction [advisor:Nima Fazeli].

Are you planning to take PhD students for Fall 2027? I would be glad to share my CV and discuss further.

Sincerely,
Arjun Mehta
